Where this comes from

I have always seen more than what was in front of me. Not because life was generous, but because imagining the next thing was how we got through this one.

I did not learn business in a classroom. I learned it standing beside my mother, selling whatever could be sold that day.

That taught me two things I have never lost. Value is usually sitting somewhere everyone else has walked past. And nothing changes until somebody decides to be responsible for it.

Everything since has been a version of that. I spent nearly twenty years turning other people's ideas into experiences, then started turning my own into companies. I am not writing this from a finish line. I am writing it from the middle of the work.

The story

Six chapters. Not a résumé — the sequence that made the founder before it made the companies.

01

The market

My first classroom did not have walls. My mother sold vegetables, fruit, newspapers, scrap — whatever could put food on the table that day. Survival was not a goal in our house. It was the daily job.

I was the child who could not sit still for a worksheet but could walk through a market and tell you in seconds what would sell, who would buy it, and how to turn a pile of scrap into cash by the weekend. Nobody graded that. So for years I never counted it as intelligence.

There was no report card for spotting an opportunity nobody else saw.
02

From the ground up

I came into the events and experience industry at the bottom and stayed nearly twenty years. I learned it from the floor: the build nights, the last-minute changes, the crew who carry the thing when the plan falls apart.

You cannot fake that knowledge later. It is why I can still walk onto a site and know within a minute whether it will hold.

The work taught me more than any title ever did.
03

Becoming a mother

I was raised by a mother who worked harder than anyone I knew. I now raise three children of my own, mostly on my own.

It did not make my ambition smaller. It made it specific. There were three people watching how I responded to pressure, to failure, to being underestimated. That is a powerful reason to keep going, and an uncomfortable one to ignore.

Responsibility did not make me careful. It made me brave.
04

Building through chaos

Very intelligent. Needs to focus. Great potential, lacks consistency. I saw some version of that sentence on my report card every year, and eventually I believed it. Scattered. Too much. Never quite enough.

It took two decades of businesses, failures and restarts to understand that the brain being criticised was the same brain doing the building. I did not fix it. I stopped trying to, and started designing around it.

Different is not broken. It just came without the manual.
05

Becoming a founder

Eventually I stopped executing other people's visions and took responsibility for my own. Gignius Middle East came first — experiences and activations for brands, venues and government entities across the UAE, delivered end to end.

There were rejections, difficult restarts and seasons where I questioned all of it. I kept building anyway, usually because I could not stop seeing what was possible.

I did not build because I had it figured out. I built because I could not unsee what was missing.
06

What comes next

Twenty years of gathering people taught me what happens after. The lights go off, everyone leaves, and almost everything that was built between them disappears with the crowd.

That is the problem I am working on now, through LYNQ Global: infrastructure that lets participation, relationships and opportunity continue past a single night, a single venue, a single city.

I am interested in what remains after the lights go off.
I am not writing from the finish line. I am still building.
Marlyn Lopez

Three words I have to keep earning

Founder. Innovator. Dreamer.

I take responsibility for making the idea real.

Anyone can spot a gap. A founder is the person who accepts what it costs to close it: the payroll, the deadline, the crew waiting on a decision at two in the morning. I have built companies from nothing more than an idea and the willingness to be accountable for it.

I notice the distance between what exists and what people actually need.

Twenty years on live sites taught me where the industry quietly wastes itself. The systems that never speak to each other, the information lost between teams, the connection that evaporates the moment an event ends. Innovation, for me, is not invention. It is refusing to accept a broken norm.

I hold on to a possibility long enough to give it a chance to exist.

I was the girl with too many ideas and not enough proof. I have learned that dreaming is not the soft part of this work. It is the part that keeps you building through the year when nobody believes you yet.

What I am building now

An infrastructure that connects people and communities, experiences and technology — all together.

We spend enormous energy bringing people together. Then it ends, and we let everything built inside that moment disappear.

The relationships. The discoveries. The people who would have collaborated, hired each other, become customers, become friends. Every event starts again from zero, and so does everyone in it.

I am not trying to make a better event. I am trying to make sure a moment does not have to be the end of something.

  • ParticipateShow up and be part of it, not just present at it
  • DiscoverFind the people, places and opportunities you came for
  • BelongBecome part of a community rather than an audience
  • ContinueCarry the connection past the venue, the night, the city

What I hold to

Beliefs

01

Challenges should not define you. They should refine you.Most of what I am useful for was built in the years I would not have chosen.

02

Different is not broken.I spent decades trying to run someone else's manual. The moment I stopped, the same traits started building things.

03

Relentless action beats perfect planning.Speed is the advantage nobody can copy. Ten attempts teach you more than the flawless plan you never started.

04

Curiosity only counts when it makes something.Ideas are cheap and I have too many. The discipline is finishing one.

05

An experience should not end when the lights go off.If nothing remains afterwards, we did not build anything. We threw a party.

06

Success means more when it opens a door for someone else.Doors opened late for me. I would rather the next person did not have to wait as long.

07

The people who believed before there was proof are part of the story.Every founder has a short list of them. Mine knows who they are.

The book

Built by Chaos

How ADHD, curiosity and relentless action turned me into a millionaire.

This is the part a founder profile usually leaves out. The unfinished projects, the money chaos, the crashes, the lonely stretches, and the slow realisation that the traits causing the most trouble were the ones doing the building.

It is not a productivity book and it is not a success story with the hard parts removed. It is a manual for a mind that works differently, written by someone who has spent her whole life inside one.

  • Your attention follows interest, not importanceStop moralising about focus and start engineering the conditions that produce it.
  • Hyperfocus is a resource, not an accidentA week of work in an afternoon, if you learn what switches it on.
  • Systems beat disciplineDesign around the person you actually are, not the one the planner was written for.

For founders, mothers, late starters and anyone who was told they were too much, too scattered, or not disciplined enough.

Impact beyond business

YEP! Young Entrepreneur Program

My first classroom was a market. I want young people to discover much earlier than I did that they are allowed to imagine something, make it, sell it, lead it and build it.

YEP! teaches children how to dream and then how to act on it: a real idea, real customers, real money changing hands. Not a lecture about entrepreneurship. The experience of being trusted with one.

Of everything I have built, this is the work I would go back to tomorrow.

The companies are part of what I build. My children are part of why I keep building.

I am raising three children while running companies, and I have stopped pretending those two things sit neatly beside each other. Some weeks one takes everything the other needed.

What I can say is this. They have watched me start again more than once, and they have never seen me stop. If they take one thing from all of it, I hope it is that.

If you are building something that can outlast a single moment, I want to hear about it.

I am always open to conversations with people building across communities, industries and borders.
